author: claude
title: How Much Risk Can You Take?

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Financial advisers often ask about risk tolerance. What does that mean?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: It's how much ups and downs in your investments you can handle, both financially and emotionally. Some people can watch their portfolio fall twenty percent and stay calm. Others can't sleep.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: How do you figure out your own risk tolerance?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: One way is to imagine a bad year. Say you invested one million yen, and a year later it's worth seven hundred thousand. Would you sell everything, do nothing, or buy more? Your honest answer tells you a lot.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: A lot, because of your time horizon. That's how long until you need the money. If you're thirty and saving for retirement, you have decades to recover from a crash. If you need the money in two years for a house, a big drop could be a disaster.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: So younger people can take more risk.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Generally, yes. They can hold more stocks, which have more volatility, meaning bigger price swings, but higher expected long-term growth.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Is it okay to choose a lower-risk plan, even if you're young?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Absolutely. The best plan is the one you can stick with. A slightly lower-risk portfolio that you keep through bad times is much better than an aggressive one that you sell in a panic.
